clinicalPearls: The most common cyanotic congenital heart lesion beyond infancy, comprising four features: a large ventricular septal defect, an overriding aorta, right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, and right ventricular hypertrophy.
The degree of cyanosis reflects the severity of right ventricular outflow obstruction; some infants are minimally cyanotic (so-called pink Fallot) while others present with marked desaturation.

A harsh systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border arises from the outflow obstruction, not from the septal defect itself; the murmur softens during a hypercyanotic spell as flow across the outflow tract falls.
Hypercyanotic (tet) spells are episodes of sudden, worsening cyanosis with agitation and deep breathing, often on waking or after feeding or crying, and can be life-threatening.

Calming manoeuvres for a spell aim to increase systemic vascular resistance and outflow through the lungs: comforting the child, bringing the knees to the chest, and giving oxygen, with pharmacological support as needed.
The chest radiograph classically shows a boot-shaped heart with a concave main pulmonary artery segment and normal or reduced pulmonary vascularity.
Echocardiography confirms the anatomy and defines the outflow tract, pulmonary arteries, and coronary artery course before surgery.
Older, unrepaired children may adopt squatting to relieve exertional cyanosis by transiently raising systemic resistance and pulmonary blood flow.
Complete surgical repair, involving closure of the septal defect and relief of outflow obstruction, is the definitive treatment and is usually performed in infancy.
reference.pathophysiology: Anterior and cephalad deviation of the infundibular septum during development produces right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, a malaligned ventricular septal defect, and an aorta that overrides the defect. Obstruction to pulmonary outflow, combined with the large communication between the ventricles, allows deoxygenated right ventricular blood to shunt right-to-left into the aorta, producing systemic desaturation. The volume of pulmonary blood flow and the resulting cyanosis depend dynamically on the balance between the fixed and dynamic outflow obstruction and systemic vascular resistance; a fall in systemic resistance or a spasm of the infundibulum increases right-to-left shunting and precipitates a hypercyanotic spell.
additionalDifferentials: Pulmonary atresia with ventricular septal defect
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography to define the outflow tract, septal defect, aortic override, and pulmonary artery anatomy
Chest radiograph looking for a boot-shaped heart and pulmonary vascularity
Electrocardiogram showing right axis deviation and right ventricular hypertrophy
Pulse oximetry and, in spells, assessment of acidosis
Cardiac catheterisation or CT/MR angiography when coronary or pulmonary artery anatomy is unclear
Genetic evaluation for 22q11.2 deletion when associated features are present
redFlags: Hypercyanotic (tet) spell with deepening cyanosis, agitation, and a disappearing murmur
Loss of consciousness, seizures, or limpness during a spell
Duct-dependent presentation with severe outflow obstruction and cardiovascular collapse as the ductus closes
Profound or worsening hypoxaemia unresponsive to calming measures
Metabolic acidosis indicating inadequate pulmonary blood flow
reference.prognosis: With timely complete surgical repair the long-term outlook is generally good, though survivors need lifelong cardiology follow-up for pulmonary regurgitation, residual outflow obstruction, arrhythmia, and possible need for pulmonary valve replacement. Untreated disease carries high morbidity and mortality from progressive cyanosis, spells, and complications.
pitfalls: Interpreting a softening or absent murmur reassuringly when it actually signals a severe hypercyanotic spell
Aggressively sedating or agitating an infant in a spell rather than using calming, resistance-raising manoeuvres
Overlooking a duct-dependent lesion in a neonate whose cyanosis worsens as the ductus arteriosus closes
Attributing exertional symptoms or squatting in an older child to behaviour rather than underlying cyanotic heart disease
Failing to screen for associated 22q11.2 deletion and other anomalies
management: Complete surgical repair — closure of the ventricular septal defect and relief of right ventricular outflow tract obstruction — is the definitive treatment, with a palliative systemic-to-pulmonary (Blalock-Taussig) shunt in neonates unsuitable for early repair
In duct-dependent presentation maintain ductal patency with a prostaglandin infusion until intervention

Abort a hypercyanotic spell by placing the child knee-to-chest, giving oxygen, opioid sedation and fluids, and a vasopressor (phenylephrine) or beta-blocker to raise systemic resistance and relax the infundibulum, correcting any metabolic acidosis
Prophylactic beta-blockade may reduce infundibular spasm and the frequency of spells while awaiting repair
Lifelong cardiology surveillance with echocardiography for pulmonary regurgitation, residual outflow obstruction and arrhythmia
Timely pulmonary valve replacement for significant pulmonary regurgitation, with electrophysiological assessment for ventricular arrhythmia
Infective endocarditis prophylaxis and coordinated transition from paediatric to adult congenital cardiology follow-up
Genetic testing and counselling for 22q11.2 deletion when associated features are present
